paper.title_en: Optical appearance and radial stability of thin-shell wormholes in fractional-power magnetic electrodynamics
paper.abstract_en: We investigate disk images of symmetric thin-shell wormholes in fractional-power magnetic electrodynamics and relate optical appearance to local radial stability. Finite magnetic self-energy fixes the seed mass and links the charge to the nonlinear scale. Transparent disks illuminate both exteriors, and independent Maxwell rays reach a static observer. For the standard Born--Infeld magnetic subset, static emitters are compared with circular motion outside the innermost stable orbit and an inward plunge below it. The wormhole--black-hole intensity difference separates light transmitted from the opposite disk from emission removed by throat excision. The illuminated inner edge depends on the admitted disk crossings rather than the throat radius alone. Increasing charge contracts the critical curve in the sampled family. Motion suppresses the face-on intensities and produces an azimuthal brightness contrast at inclination. A broad outer shoulder arises from partial compensation between decreasing emissivity and increasing circular frequency weights, before the profiles recover a decaying weak-field tail. All nine prescribed throats satisfy a local radial stability test for a calibrated modified cosmic Chaplygin law describing an effective exotic layer. An analytic identity establishes radial instability at the selected unstable photon orbit for any finite density-only constitutive slope. The resulting images relate transmitted radiation and emitter kinematics to the material support of the throat, providing a controlled comparison with the matched seed black hole.
